title: Soft Quality-Diversity Optimization
claim: Discrete archives fully credit each region to one occupant; our soft formulation gives each solution a smooth, discretization-independent influence field.
layout: 2 panels side by side, shared colormap, Voronoi cells versus smooth field
description: Two square heatmaps sit side by side, each with a viridis colorbar from 0 to 100. The left panel shows a discrete archive as a Voronoi tessellation. Each cell is filled with one flat color set by its occupant's quality, and white dots mark the solutions. Many cells are dark purple, meaning empty or low quality. The colorbar is labeled f(θ). The right panel uses the same points and the same Voronoi boundaries, now drawn as faint dashed white lines. The fill is a smooth glowing field. Each solution radiates intensity that fades with distance, and the brightest yellow-green blobs sit around the high-quality points. The colorbar is labeled v_θ(b). The eye goes first to the bright yellow patches and the contrast between blocky cells and the smooth gradient.
caption: Left: In a discrete archive, each cell is fully illuminated by its highest-quality occupant. Right: In Soft QD, each solution illuminates the area around with an intensity proportional to its quality. The smooth scalar field defined by the behavior value $v_{\btheta}(b)$ is independent of discretization.
abstract: Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms constitute a branch of optimization that is concerned with discovering a diverse and high-quality set of solutions to an optimization problem. Current QD methods commonly maintain diversity by dividing the behavior space into discrete regions, ensuring that solutions are distributed across different parts of the space. The QD problem is then solved by searching for the best solution in each region. This approach to QD optimization poses challenges in large solution spaces, where storing many solutions is impractical, and in high-dimensional behavior spaces, where discretization becomes ineffective due to the curse of dimensionality. We present an alternative framing of the QD problem, called \emph{Soft QD}, that sidesteps the need for discretizations. We validate this formulation by demonstrating its desirable properties, such as monotonicity, and by relating its limiting behavior to the widely used QD Score metric. Furthermore, we leverage it to derive a novel differentiable QD algorithm, \emph{Soft QD Using Approximated Diversity (SQUAD)}, and demonstrate empirically that it is competitive with current state of the art methods on standard benchmarks while offering better scalability to higher dimensional problems. Source code is available at https://github.com/conflictednerd/soft-qd.
